Our static-site releases happen in two steps: first we upload the new assets under versioned names, then we switch the manifest to point at them.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells a browser which asset files to load. As soon as it changes, every new visitor starts requesting the names it lists. If we switched the manifest before the upload finished, those browsers would ask for files that don't exist yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references is already in place when the manifest goes live. Because each release uses new versioned names, the upload never overwrites anything currently in use, so users see no change until the switch.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that fetched the previous manifest before the switch still has the old names and will keep requesting them. If we deleted the old files, those visitors would hit missing assets partway through their session. Keeping the old assets available lets them finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new release.

Every release is two steps: upload the new assets under new versioned names, then point the manifest at them. The old assets stay up afterward.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment users start getting the new release. If it happened before the upload, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request assets that don't exist yet, giving it broken pages or missing scripts. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to is already there when the manifest goes live. Because each version uses its own names, the upload doesn't touch anything the current release is serving.

**Why the old assets stay:** The switch doesn't reach browsers that already loaded the previous manifest. Those sessions keep requesting the old names, for example when they lazy-load a chunk or navigate to another page. If those files were deleted, those users would hit missing assets in the middle of a session. Keeping them available lets every browser finish with a consistent set of files from whichever release it started on.

The result is that no client ever sees a manifest pointing at files that aren't there, whether those files are new or old.

Here's the process. Every release has two steps, and they always run in this order.

**1. Upload the new assets under versioned names.** Each new file gets a name that's unique to its version, so it never overwrites anything already live.

**2. Switch the manifest to point at the new names.** The manifest tells browsers which asset files to load. Changing it is what actually makes the release live.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest switches, browsers immediately start requesting the files it names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, the requests fail and users get a broken page. When everything is uploaded first, every name in the new manifest already resolves. That makes the switch a single, clean cutover instead of a race between the manifest and the uploads.

**Why we keep the old assets:** some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and are still running from it. That manifest names the old files, so those browsers will keep requesting them. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit missing assets partway through their session. Keeping the old files means both the previous and the current manifest work at the same time. Old sessions finish on the old version, and new sessions load the new one.

Versioned names are what make this possible. Old and new files never share a name, so they can sit side by side without overwriting each other.

Our releases happen in two steps: upload, then switch.

**1. Upload the new assets under versioned names.** Every file in the new build gets a name unique to that version, so nothing already live is overwritten. At this point the new files exist, but nothing references them yet, so users see no change.

**2. Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells browsers which asset files make up the site. Updating it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest points at the new names, any browser that loads it will immediately request those files. If any file isn't uploaded yet, that request fails and the page loads broken. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. Because the names are versioned, the upload can't disturb the live site while it runs.

**Why we keep the old assets:** switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers keep requesting the old file names for as long as they run that version of the site. If we deleted the old assets, those requests would fail and break pages for people who were already using the site when we released. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish normally while new visitors get the new version.
